title: Event Loop: The Full Picture
concept: Even in complex async code, you can precisely predict the execution order

steps.title: Register setTimeout
steps.explanation: The `setTimeout` callback is delegated to the Web API and then moves to the **Task Queue** to wait.

steps.title: Register the First .then
steps.explanation: The callback from the first `.then()` is added to the **Microtask Queue**.

steps.title: Synchronous Code #2
steps.explanation:
The last synchronous line `console.log('5')` executes.
All synchronous code is now complete and the call stack is empty.

steps.title: Microtask #1 Executes
steps.explanation:
With the call stack empty, the event loop checks the Microtask Queue first.
The first callback runs and prints '3'. The Promise it returns causes the next `.then` callback to be **newly added** to the Microtask Queue.
steps.keyInsight: Promise chaining adds new Microtasks to the queue.

steps.title: Microtask #2 Executes
steps.explanation:
The event loop keeps checking the Microtask Queue until it's completely empty.
The newly added second callback runs and prints '4'.

steps.title: Task Executes
steps.explanation:
Only once the Microtask Queue is finally empty does the event loop check the Task Queue.
The `setTimeout` callback runs and prints '2' last.

quiz.explanation:
1) Synchronous: print D
2) Microtask: print B, add new Microtask (C)
3) New Microtask: print C (keeps running until Microtask Queue is empty)
4) Task: print A

misconceptions.wrong: Microtasks run one at a time and then hand off to Tasks
misconceptions.correct: The event loop keeps running Microtasks until the Microtask Queue is **completely empty (0 items)**.
misconceptions.why:
While you're in line, a new friend (Promise chaining) can jump right behind you in that same line.
Only when that entire line is gone can the process move on to the next stage (Rendering, Task Queue, etc.).

keyTakeaway: Execution priority: synchronous code > Microtask (Promise) > Task (setTimeout)
